Workshop.title: Advocacy challenges
Workshop.subtitle: Fifteen real advocacy and lobbying challenges, from lower to higher complexity, to work through as a group.
Workshop.howItWorks: Each challenge is an advocacy problem, not an exercise about the app. Pick one, decide the strategy, and use PATHSapp to structure it: who decides, who can help, what actions, what deadlines, and how you'll know it worked. Tick the box once your group has worked it through.
Workshop.backToApp: Open the app to work on it

BEGINNER.name: Lower complexity
BEGINNER.hint: One counterpart, local scope, short cycle. Achievable in weeks or a few months, and the result is easy to verify.

INTERMEDIATE.name: Medium complexity
INTERMEDIATE.hint: Several actors with competing interests, provincial or national sector scope. Needs technical evidence, allies, and a one- to two-year cycle.

ADVANCED.name: High complexity
ADVANCED.hint: Active resistance, public money at stake, national or regional scope. Requires a coalition, several parallel tracks, and surviving changes of government.

b1.title: From informal acquaintance to recognized counterpart
b1.task: Your association only talks to the head of haematology at the referral hospital when there's an emergency, over WhatsApp and on a personal basis. The challenge is to secure a first formal meeting, with minutes or a confirming email, establishing a stable channel.
b1.doneWhen: There's no opposition, but no urgency for the other side either: nobody says no, they just don't reply. The real challenge is persistence without burning the relationship by pushing badly.
b1.why: An Action-type goal. The department head is the one it “depends on”. Log every attempt (call, email, encounter) to see how many it took — that number is useful next time.

b2.title: Making factor pickup hours public knowledge
b2.task: Families aren't sure of the factor bank's opening hours or who to call if it runs out after hours, and the information travels by word of mouth. The challenge is getting the hospital to publish it officially and accessibly.
b2.doneWhen: It looks trivial, but it hits diffuse responsibility: pharmacy says it's the department's, the department says it's communications'. You have to find who actually signs off.
b2.why: This is where tracking offices rather than just people pays off: you'll bounce between areas until you find the one with the mandate. Log each hand-off.

b3.title: How many of us there are, according to the State
b3.task: There's no official count of people with haemophilia in your jurisdiction, or the one that exists is visibly lower than your own membership list. The challenge is getting the health authority's figure in writing, however bad it is.
b3.doneWhen: Asking for a figure is easy; getting it in writing is the hard part. And if it comes back very low, you have to decide whether to call it out publicly or use it quietly as leverage.
b3.why: The official figure is your baseline: store it as an indicator. The gap between their number and yours is the argument behind almost everything that follows.

b4.title: Making 17 April exist for the authorities
b4.task: World Haemophilia Day is marked by your association alone. The challenge is getting the local health authority to take it on: an official statement, lighting up a public building, or a joint activity.
b4.doneWhen: It's a low political cost ask, so it usually lands. The difficulty is the calendar: ask in March and you've missed their internal processes.
b4.why: Perfect for the strategic calendar: it's a recurring date. And for duplicating the goal as a template, since you'll run it again every year.

b5.title: A seat at a table that already exists
b5.task: There's an existing health advisory council, participation forum, or patient committee, with nobody representing bleeding disorders. The challenge is getting that seat, even as a non-voting guest.
b5.doneWhen: There's rarely a clear public call for applications: you get in through contacts. And once in, attendance has to be sustained with volunteers.
b5.why: A clear “door-opener” case: log which contact can introduce you to whoever decides that forum's composition.

i1.title: Making sure supply doesn't break again
i1.task: Last year there were two factor stockouts: one of three weeks, another of six. The challenge is securing a formal minimum-stock commitment and an early-warning mechanism that tells you before it runs out, not after.
i1.doneWhen: Nobody defends a stockout, but the cause is split between procurement, budget, customs, and the supplier. Each area refers you to the next, and you have to document the clinical harm without exposing personal stories.
i1.why: A challenge with many counterparts: use each one's stance to see where you have allies and where you don't. Log the commitments they make to you, with follow-up dates, because this is exactly the kind of promise that gets forgotten.

i2.title: A registry that's actually usable for planning
i2.task: There's no national bleeding disorders registry, or it exists on paper with no budget or staff. The challenge is getting it created or reactivated, with an allocated budget line and a named owner.
i2.doneWhen: Everyone agrees in the abstract and nobody wants to pay for it. It also collides with data protection, and you have to get into next year's budget cycle, not this one's.
i2.why: Here the strategic calendar rules: miss the window before the draft budget closes and you lose a year. Mark that window.

i3.title: From treating bleeds to preventing them
i3.task: The current protocol covers on-demand treatment; prophylaxis is applied at each centre's and clinician's discretion. The challenge is getting prophylaxis recognized in the national clinical guideline or protocol.
i3.doneWhen: It's a technical debate where your association isn't the expert voice: you need the scientific society to lead. And the short-term cost argument works against you, even though the long-term one works for you.
i3.why: The versioned-petition challenge: your text will shift with whatever the scientific society will endorse. And joint letters, because you won't win this one alone.

i4.title: Comprehensive treatment centres, not scattered care
i4.task: People with haemophilia are seen at whichever hospital is nearest, with no experienced haematologist and no coordinated physiotherapy or dentistry. The challenge is getting accredited comprehensive treatment centres formally recognized.
i4.doneWhen: Concentrating care means some hospitals lose patients and budget — that's where the real resistance appears, and it comes from inside the system. It also worsens access for families living far away unless travel is solved too.
i4.why: Note that this challenge creates opposition: use the “opposed” stance without hesitation, and log the history when someone shifts position.

i5.title: Living far away shouldn't cost you treatment
i5.task: Families in the interior spend more than they can afford on fares and lodging to reach the referral centre, and some simply stop going. The challenge is getting travel and accommodation covered.
i5.doneWhen: This isn't a health ask, it's social assistance or transport, so your usual counterpart has no mandate. You have to open a new door in a ministry you have no relationship with.
i5.why: A case where the contact graph beats the contact list: find who in your directory can introduce you to someone on the social side.

a1.title: Getting onto the national medicines list
a1.task: An extended half-life or non-factor therapy is available in the country but isn't on the national essential medicines list (formulary, basic basket, or local equivalent). The challenge is getting it included with public coverage.
a1.doneWhen: The hardest and longest challenge: it has to clear a health technology assessment on cost-effectiveness criteria, and even when approved it can be blocked on budget. It's measured in years, not months, and the price is set by someone who isn't at the table.
a1.why: This needs everything: a versioned petition, clinical and economic evidence attached, a stance map of the assessment committee, and the outcome chain so you can explain afterwards how it was won.

a2.title: Reversing a cut that's already decided
a2.task: The health authority has just reduced coverage you already had: fewer units per patient, or an age group excluded. The challenge is getting it restored.
a2.doneWhen: You're on the defensive with the clock against you. Three tracks have to open at once (administrative, judicial, and public via the press) knowing the public track can slam the negotiating door shut. Deciding how much noise to make is the strategic call.
a2.why: A deadline challenge: the administrative appeal has a hard cut-off. And a media coverage one: log every appearance and its tone, because you'll have to justify the strategy later.

a3.title: Buying together to pay less
a3.task: Your country buys factor in small volumes and pays far more than neighbouring countries. The challenge is pushing for regional joint procurement, or for use of an existing mechanism such as the PAHO Strategic Fund or a sub-regional joint negotiation.
a3.doneWhen: Your counterpart stops being your ministry and becomes a multilateral body you have no direct access to. You need associations in several countries asking for the same thing at the same time, coordinating with no shared structure and on different political calendars.
a3.why: The joint-letter challenge par excellence: several organizations, each at a different signing stage, against a shared deadline you can't move.

a4.title: A law that outlives the government that passed it
a4.task: Haemophilia appears in no national rare disease policy, or appears with no earmarked budget. The challenge is getting it into the legislation with allocated funding, and keeping it there after an election.
a4.doneWhen: The cycle is longer than a term of office. Your counterparts change midway and the relationship has to be rebuilt from scratch with whoever arrives, often without the administration having handed over the file.
a4.why: The challenge that justifies tracking offices, not just people: when the holder changes, the record of who was there before and what was agreed is all you have left.

a5.title: The women the system doesn't count
a5.task: Symptomatic carriers and women with haemophilia aren't recognized in the regulations, can't access diagnosis or treatment, and don't even appear in many registries. The challenge is changing the definition the system itself uses.
a5.doneWhen: You're not asking for a resource: you're asking for recognition of a group that officially doesn't exist, so there's no baseline to argue from. And it collides with the established clinical belief that haemophilia is a male condition, even among allied professionals.
a5.why: The hardest one to measure: think about what indicator you could build when the starting point is zero on record, and use the media coverage log, because this is a challenge won partly by changing the public conversation.
